Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s assessment

**The Seller’s package materially shifts risk to Wattlebridge.** It combines broad disclosure and deemed buyer knowledge with low liability limits, then seeks to apply those protections to virtually every claim—including title, specific indemnities and potentially failure to perform completion obligations.

The immediate priorities are **effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment and security releases, correct treatment of completion bonuses, and resolution of Ironquay’s IP ownership conditions**.

This review is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the complete SPA or underlying DD documents. References to those documents are therefore matters to verify, not independently established facts.

## 1. Liability protections: reject a single regime for all claims

### General warranty cap and thresholds

The proposed **AUD 4.8 million cap (20%)**, AUD 25,000 de minimis and **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** substantially restrict recovery. Once the basket is exceeded, the Buyer still bears the first AUD 250,000; smaller claims may never qualify.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher general warranty cap, informed by outstanding diligence, seller covenant strength and any warranty insurance.
- Reduce the de minimis and basket, and seek a **tipping basket**, so qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar once the threshold is reached.
- Aggregate claims arising from the same or related circumstances to prevent artificial fragmentation.
- Specify which claims count towards the basket and cap.

These figures are negotiating positions, not inherently invalid terms. Their acceptability depends on the other protections obtained.

### Fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities

“Administrative simplicity” is not a sound reason to give title and capacity warranties the same protection as ordinary business warranties. The Buyer could otherwise pay AUD 24 million without obtaining good title and have contractual recovery limited to AUD 4.8 million.

**Push back:**
- Give title, capacity and authority warranties a separate cap of at least the purchase price and a substantially longer claim period, without general warranty thresholds.
- Negotiate a separate tax covenant/indemnity and tax warranties, with periods aligned to relevant assessment and reopening risks.
- Give each specific indemnity its own appropriate scope, cap and survival period.
- Exclude purchase-price adjustments, debt repayment, leakage and completion obligations from general warranty limitations.
- Expressly preserve fraud and fraudulent concealment claims; negotiate appropriate treatment of wilful misconduct.

The Seller’s assertion that tax and IP are “settled” should not be accepted without confirming the Buyer actually agreed those positions.

### Time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance

Eighteen months may leave insufficient time to identify latent problems, including through subsequent accounts or audits. More importantly, applying all limitations to **“all Claims of any nature”** could neutralise the separate protections negotiated elsewhere.

**Push back:**
- Seek a longer general warranty notification period, for example 24–36 months, with separate periods for fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity claims.
- Ensure timely notification preserves a claim; reject unreasonable requirements to quantify it fully or commence proceedings immediately.
- Review clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 together so exclusive-remedy and non-reliance language cannot override express indemnities, completion obligations or agreed remedies.
- Preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded, including applicable statutory rights. Do not assume a broad non-reliance clause is either wholly effective or harmless under NSW/Australian law.

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge: reject constructive knowledge

General disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, accounts and public records is exceptionally broad. Clause 8.3 compounds this by barring claims for anything the Buyer **or its advisers could have discovered**.

The practical result could be that scattered documents defeat a claim even though they never fairly explained the problem.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, linked to the relevant warranty.
- Delete blanket disclosure of referenced material and public records, or narrowly specify any agreed exceptions.
- Freeze and retain the agreed indexed data-room archive; control subsequent disclosures and their effect.
- Delete the buyer-knowledge exclusion or limit it to actual knowledge of specified individuals, without constructive or imputed adviser knowledge.
- State expressly that disclosure and buyer knowledge do not qualify specific indemnities or obligations to resolve identified matters.

A disclosed risk is not necessarily an accepted risk. Disclosure should not excuse repayment, obtaining consent or delivering title.

## 3. Bluefen: require effective consent, not merely a consent document

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. No final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been provided. A reasonable-endeavours obligation does not deliver the commercial outcome the Buyer needs.

**Push back:**
- Make effective change-of-control consent a Buyer-protective condition precedent.
- Require compliance with clause 11.3 and any conditions in the consent itself, not simply delivery of a letter.
- Require the consent to cover the actual transaction and avoid unacceptable fees, adverse contract changes or termination rights.
- Give the Buyer control over waiver of this condition and an appropriate termination right if it is not satisfied by the long-stop date.

The Seller’s statement that consent is “addressed” is not supported by its own disclosure.

## 4. Riverlark: no post-completion release gap

The approximately **AUD 3.2 million facility remains outstanding**, and no final security discharge is included. A promised release after Completion leaves the Buyer owning a company with unresolved debt and security exposure.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a binding payout letter, including accrued interest, fees and discharge mechanics.
- Repay the facility through the completion funds flow, with effective release arrangements at Completion and prompt completion of necessary registry removals.
- Address change-of-control requirements, related guarantees and any other secured obligations.
- Reflect the debt in the **AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free mechanics**, unless the Seller discharges it separately, without double counting.

A later administrative registration step may be manageable; an unsecured promise to procure a release later is not equivalent protection.

## 5. Completion bonuses: allocate the full cost expressly

The **AUD 420,000 bonuses** are conditional, so the materials do not establish an unconditional current liability. Nevertheless, they appear transaction-triggered and are missing from the funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the Company becoming liable.

**Push back:**
- Confirm who owes the bonuses, when entitlement arises and how continued-employment conditions operate.
- Allocate seller-agreed transaction bonuses to the Seller through payment, a price deduction or a specific indemnity, as appropriate.
- Quantify any applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other employer on-costs.
- Show the agreed treatment expressly in the funds flow and price definitions, avoiding both omission and double recovery.

## 6. Ironquay: protect ownership and use of the IP, not just the invoice

The identified risk is not merely an **AUD 180,000 payment**. Transfer of SOW3 materials is conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The open balance is not conclusive proof of non-payment, but neither payment nor an effective assignment has been established.

**Push back:**
- Verify the complete SOW3 payment position and obtain reliable payment evidence.
- Require satisfaction of transfer conditions and a confirmatory assignment or acknowledgement of ownership, addressing relevant IP rights and necessary consents.
- Review the broader development agreement and chain of title.
- Expand the indemnity beyond the specified payment to losses from defective ownership, third-party claims, interruption and necessary remediation arising from the identified issue.

Payment of one invoice alone may not resolve all ownership requirements.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: unresolved, not immaterial or confirmed

The evidence describes a link sent to an unintended external address, potentially involving **about 1,240 records**. It does **not** establish unauthorised access, a notifiable breach or quantified loss. Equally, the Seller has no demonstrated basis to dismiss it as immaterial.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation of access logs, link permissions, recipients, affected information, containment and deletion.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual, security and notification obligations; do not assume notification is required—or unnecessary.
- Require ongoing information and appropriate consultation on remediation and communications, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-completion incident and appropriate completion protection if findings materially worsen the risk.

Any indemnity should address investigation, remediation and third-party exposure, subject to legal limits on recoverability.

## 8. Sandbar renewals: establish their economic substance

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither “ordinary course” nor their aggregate value establishes the correct price treatment.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together to establish commitment dates, service periods, cancellation rights, accruals and commercial necessity.
- Test compliance with interim operating covenants and any aggregate commitment thresholds.
- Allocate costs under the agreed debt, working-capital, transaction-cost or leakage definitions according to their substance.

Do not automatically deduct the entire amount: future ordinary-course services may properly be a Buyer cost. Equally, seller-period liabilities or exceptional commitments should not escape adjustment merely because they are called renewals.

## 9. Title, lease and Mossvale: verify without overstating

- **Share title:** DD-012 supports registered ownership, but is not complete verification of beneficial ownership, encumbrances or competing rights. Check the constitution, capital and transfer records, options and other equity rights, relevant searches and required transfer documents. Require title to all shares free of encumbrances at Completion.
- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies a **notification obligation**, not landlord consent. Require compliant notification and check the full lease.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not automatically apply to a share sale. Review the complete contract for change-of-control provisions; do not demand consent solely on the quoted restriction.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure completion outcomes:** effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark payout and release arrangements; verified share title; resolved Ironquay transfer conditions.
2. **Fix the economics:** reconcile debt, bonuses and on-costs, and supplier commitments through explicit, non-duplicative price and funds-flow treatment.
3. **Rebuild recourse:** separate fundamental, tax, specific-indemnity and completion claims from general warranty limitations.
4. **Reject blanket risk transfer:** narrow general disclosure, constructive knowledge, non-reliance and all-claims limitations.
5. **Investigate and allocate unresolved risks:** particularly the export incident and Ironquay IP, supported by specific contractual protection and credible recovery security where needed.

**Do not trade essential completion protections for a higher warranty cap:** damages after Completion are a poor substitute for retaining a major customer, acquiring usable IP and receiving a debt-free company.
